t: Economic strain, the Perry Expedition and the unequal treaties that followed undermined the Tokugawa shogunate, and many lower and middle-ranking samurai became shishi, “men of spirit”, devoted to the Emperor.

Led by Satsuma and Chōshū, an alliance of domains overthrew the shogunal system; on 3 January 1868 Emperor Meiji declared political power restored to the Imperial House, and the Boshin War ended Tokugawa resistance.
The new government abolished the domains and the samurai class, built schools, a conscript army and industries, and laid the foundations of the Empire of Japan.
dyk: Sakamoto Ryōma first went to Katsu Kaishū intending to assassinate him for his pro-foreign views; instead Katsu won him over to his plan for rearmament, and Sakamoto followed him to the Kobe Naval Training Centre.
ev: Commodore Matthew C. Perry’s American expedition reaches Japan with documents requesting an end to Japanese isolation
Ii Naosuke approves the Treaty of Amity and Commerce against the Emperor’s wishes and launches the Ansei Purge
Sakamoto Ryōma brings Kido Takayoshi and Saigō Takamori together to form the Satsuma–Chōshū Alliance
Tokugawa Yoshinobu, the 15th shōgun, returns power to the Imperial Court and resigns the title of shōgun
Domain troops seize the Imperial Palace and the Emperor declares the restoration of his authority, setting off the Boshin War
The daimyō are told that the domains are abolished, and the 302 domains become 72 prefectures in January 1872
Nationwide conscription extends the right to bear arms, once a samurai privilege, to every man
The Meiji Constitution is adopted; it remains in place until the Allied occupation after the Second World War

f.where: Japan: Edo (renamed Tōkyō in 1868) and Kyōto; the domains of Satsuma, Chōshū, Tosa, Hizen and Mito; the treaty ports; and Hokkaidō, where the Republic of Ezo was ended.
f.period: The opening of Japan by the Perry Expedition and the unequal treaties (1853–1858); political violence and the shishi loyalists (1858–1864); the anti-Tokugawa alliance and domain rebellion (1864–1867); the shōgun’s resignation (1867) and the restoration of 3 January 1868; the Boshin War (1868–1869); the abolition of the domains (1868–1873) and of samurai stipends (1876); the Meiji Constitution (1889).
f.figures: Emperor Meiji; Tokugawa Yoshinobu, the 15th and last Tokugawa shōgun; the court noble Iwakura Tomomi; Saigō Takamori and Ōkubo Toshimichi of Satsuma; Kido Takayoshi, Takasugi Shinsaku and Itō Hirobumi of Chōshū; Sakamoto Ryōma of Tosa, who brokered the Satsuma–Chōshū Alliance; the teacher Yoshida Shōin; Katsu Kaishū, who negotiated for the Tokugawa.
f.outcome: The shogunate and feudalism ended; the 302 domains became 72 prefectures in 1872; samurai privileges were abolished and conscription introduced in 1873; Japan industrialised and was a military power by 1895; the Meiji Constitution of 1889 lasted until the Allied occupation after the Second World War.
